title: Roots
hook: Sariputta: the roots of the unwholesome are greed, hate and delusion; their opposites are the wholesome roots (MN 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma ditthi, right view, and your line, see it as it is. Did you try the four questions on something that went sideways? Day three hundred fifty-five.
screen: `SAMMA DITTHI — SEE IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Anyone who's pulled weeds knows the trick. Snap off the top and you've done nothing; next week it's back, greener than before. You have to get your fingers down into the soil and ease out the root, the pale stringy part you never see. The first answer Sariputta gives in his talk on right view is about exactly this. Before the four truths, before the twelve links, he starts with actions and the roots they grow from. Today, the word for what grows from good roots: kusala.
screen: `SNAP OFF THE TOP.` → `IT'S BACK NEXT WEEK.` → `EASE OUT THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Kusala is usually translated wholesome, or skillful. In everyday Pali it can describe someone skilled at a craft, or someone well and healthy. Its opposite is akusala: unwholesome, unskillful. Sariputta begins by naming unwholesome actions, ten of them, a list later called the ten unwholesome courses of action: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will and wrong view. Three of the body, four of speech, three of the mind. Then the roots. What is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is a root. Hatred is a root. Delusion is a root. And the wholesome? Abstaining from those ten. And its roots: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. Notice the shape. Sariputta doesn't stop at the list of actions. The ten are the weeds above the ground. The roots are what keep them coming back. You can stop lying for a week by force of will, but if the greed or fear underneath is untouched, the lie grows back. Notice too that the wholesome roots are described with a not: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. But some teachers explain them positively as well: non-greed shows up as generosity, non-hatred as kindness, non-delusion as wisdom. So a single generous act isn't only a nice thing done. It's a root being watered. And here's why Sariputta starts here, in a talk about right view. Seeing clearly begins with seeing what's actually driving what you do. Not to feel guilty about it. To know which root to tend.
screen: `KUSALA: WHOLESOME, SKILLFUL.` · `TEN UNWHOLESOME ACTIONS.` · `GREED, HATRED, DELUSION.` · `GENEROSITY, KINDNESS, WISDOM.` · then, large: `ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one root at work. Sit, and let the last day replay gently. Find one moment you acted, spoke or thought something you're not proud of, a small one. Don't scold yourself. Just look underneath it: was the root wanting, or aversion, or confusion? Then find one moment you acted well, and look under that too: generosity, kindness, or clear seeing? Rest with that root a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Kusala. Wholesome, skillful: actions rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, the roots Sariputta names first in his talk on right view.
Your line: a root being watered. Today, when you catch yourself about to say or do something you'll regret, ask which root it's growing from. Then water a different one. Day three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teaching across schools names the three unwholesome roots, greed, hatred and delusion, and the ten courses of action; some practitioners reflect at the end of the day on which roots their actions came from.

match.prompt: match each root to its opposite.

fork.setup: you've told a small lie to avoid an awkward conversation. by Sariputta's teaching, what's worth looking at?
options: the root underneath it: greed, hatred or delusion.
fork.reveal: Sariputta names the actions, then the roots they grow from; tending the root is what keeps the weed from coming back.

original.note: Pali kusala: wholesome, skillful; its opposite is akusala, unwholesome.

trapdoor: what you thought: wholesome means being a good person.
what it means: actions are wholesome or unwholesome by their roots: greed, hatred and delusion, or their opposites.
what a scholar hears: MN 9 names lobha, dosa and moha as the akusala-mūla and alobha, adosa and amoha as the kusala-mūla, and lists the ten akusala-kammapatha.

sources.ref: MN 9 (Sammaditthi Sutta), the wholesome and unwholesome and their roots

notes: MN 9 paraphrased: confirm the ten unwholesome courses and the three roots each way.
Kusala's everyday sense (skilled, healthy, well) follows PED; the commentarial kusa-grass etymology was deliberately left out.
Glossing non-greed / non-hatred / non-delusion positively as generosity / kindness (loving-kindness) / wisdom is a common Abhidhamma-based teaching; confirm.

Editor review: softened 'the list Buddhists know as', 'teachers in many schools' and the howItsDone 'many reflect each evening' to claims the sources support; no textual changes to the MN 9 paraphrase.
